cards.front: In the usual convention, \(\mathbf{i}\) is often due [ ___ ] and \(\mathbf{j}\) is often due [ ___ ].
cards.back: In the usual convention, \(\mathbf{i}\) is often due east and \(\mathbf{j}\) is often due north.

options.text: In the usual convention, \(\mathbf{i}\) is often due east and \(\mathbf{j}\) is often due north.
options.explanation: In the standard Cartesian convention, the unit vector \(\mathbf{i}\) points horizontally east and \(\mathbf{j}\) points vertically north.

options.text: In the usual convention, \(\mathbf{i}\) is often due north and \(\mathbf{j}\) is often due east.
options.explanation: The directions have been reversed. By convention, \(\mathbf{i}\) represents east and \(\mathbf{j}\) represents north, so this completion assigns both unit vectors incorrectly.

options.text: In the usual convention, \(\mathbf{i}\) is often due east and \(\mathbf{j}\) is often due south.
options.explanation: The first direction is correct, but the second is not. The standard convention uses \(\mathbf{j}\) for north, not south, so this confuses positive and negative vertical directions.

options.text: In the usual convention, \(\mathbf{i}\) is often due west and \(\mathbf{j}\) is often due north.
options.explanation: The second direction is correct, but \(\mathbf{i}\) points east rather than west. West is the negative \(\mathbf{i}\) direction, so this reverses the horizontal axis.

cards.front: What does \(3\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j}\) say about its components?
cards.back: 3 units in the \(\mathbf{i}\) direction4 units in the negative \(\mathbf{j}\) direction

options.text: 3 units in the \(\mathbf{i}\) direction4 units in the negative \(\mathbf{j}\) direction
options.explanation: The coefficient of \(\mathbf{i}\) gives 3 units in the positive \(\mathbf{i}\) direction, while the negative coefficient of \(\mathbf{j}\) gives 4 units opposite to \(\mathbf{j}\).

options.text: 3 units in the \(\mathbf{i}\) direction4 units in the \(\mathbf{j}\) direction
options.explanation: The sign of the \(\mathbf{i}\) coefficient is positive, so the first component is correct, but the second coefficient is negative. The \(\mathbf{j}\) component therefore points negatively, not positively.

options.text: 3 units in the negative \(\mathbf{i}\) direction4 units in the \(\mathbf{j}\) direction
options.explanation: The negative sign applies to the \(\mathbf{j}\) component, not the \(\mathbf{i}\) component. The correct interpretation is 3 units in \(\mathbf{i}\) and 4 units in negative \(\mathbf{j}\).

options.text: 4 units in the \(\mathbf{i}\) direction3 units in the negative \(\mathbf{j}\) direction
options.explanation: Both the signs and directions have been misread. The coefficients are 3 for positive \(\mathbf{i}\) and -4 for \(\mathbf{j}\), giving 3 units positive and 4 units negative.

cards.front: How do you find displacement from initial and final position vectors?

options.explanation: Displacement describes the change in position, so it is obtained by subtracting the initial position vector from the final position vector.
This reverses the subtraction order. Initial position minus final position gives the negative of the displacement, which points in the opposite direction.
Adding the two position vectors does not measure the change between them. Displacement requires final position minus initial position so the starting point is removed.
This uses only the final position and ignores where the particle started. Displacement must compare both positions using final minus initial.

cards.front: The speed of a particle is the [ ___ ] of its velocity vector.
cards.back: The speed of a particle is the magnitude of its velocity vector.

options.explanation: Velocity is a vector containing both speed and direction. Its magnitude removes the directional information and leaves the particle’s scalar speed.
Direction is part of velocity but not speed. Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, so it has no directional component.
A component is only one projection of a vector and may be positive, negative, or zero. Speed uses the complete vector’s magnitude instead.
Velocity is a vector, whereas speed is a scalar. Calling speed the scalar of velocity is imprecise; the required operation is taking its magnitude.

cards.front: For constant velocity, what is the position vector at time \(t\)?

options.explanation: With constant velocity, displacement from the initial position is \(\mathbf{v}t\). Adding this to \(\mathbf{r}_0\) gives the position at time \(t\).
The velocity term must be added because it represents displacement from the initial position. Subtracting it reverses the direction of motion.
This omits the initial position, so it assumes the particle starts at the origin. The general expression must include \(\mathbf{r}_0\).
Time multiplies velocity to produce displacement; it does not divide it. The correct constant-velocity relation adds \(\mathbf{v}t\) to the initial position.

cards.front: Given positions \(\mathbf{r}_1\) and \(\mathbf{r}_2\) separated by time \(\Delta t\), how do you find constant velocity?

options.explanation: Constant velocity equals displacement divided by the elapsed time. The displacement from the first position to the second is \(\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1\).
This reverses the displacement, producing the velocity in the opposite direction. The correct order is final position minus initial position: \(\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1\).
Adding positions does not give the displacement between them. Velocity requires their difference, divided by the elapsed time.
Multiplying by time gives a displacement, not a velocity. To obtain velocity, divide the displacement \(\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1\) by \(\Delta t\).

cards.front: A bearing is measured [ ___ ] from [ ___ ].
cards.back: A bearing is measured clockwise from north.

options.text: A bearing is measured clockwise from north.
options.explanation: A bearing is defined as a clockwise angle measured from north. This convention gives a unique three-figure direction for navigation and vector problems.

options.text: A bearing is measured anticlockwise from north.
options.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise, not anticlockwise. Reversing the sense of rotation would give the opposite angular convention.

options.text: A bearing is measured clockwise from east.
options.explanation: The rotation is clockwise, but the reference direction is wrong. Bearings start from north, whereas east is associated with an angle of 090°.

options.text: A bearing is measured anticlockwise from east.
options.explanation: Both parts use the wrong convention. A bearing starts at north and is measured clockwise, rather than anticlockwise from east.

cards.front: What is the bearing of velocity \(-4\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}\), to the nearest degree?

options.explanation: The vector points 4 units west and 5 units north. Its angle west of north is \(\tan^{-1}(4/5)\approx38.7^\circ\), giving bearing \(360^\circ-38.7^\circ\approx321^\circ\).
This is approximately the angle measured from the east-west axis, not a bearing from north. Bearings require clockwise measurement from north, giving \(321^\circ\).
Using \(\tan^{-1}(5/4)\) instead of \(\tan^{-1}(4/5)\) measures the wrong acute angle. The correct bearing is \(360^\circ-\tan^{-1}(4/5)\approx321^\circ\).
This places the vector in the south-east quadrant, as though the signs of both components had been mishandled. The vector is north-west, with bearing approximately \(321^\circ\).

cards.front: With constant acceleration, what vector equation links \(\mathbf{v}\), \(\mathbf{u}\), \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(t\)?

options.explanation: Under constant acceleration, the change in velocity after time $t$ is $\mathbf{a}t$. Adding this change to the initial velocity $\mathbf{u}$ gives the final velocity $\mathbf{v}$.
Subtracting $\mathbf{a}t$ reverses the effect of acceleration. With the acceleration vector defined in its actual direction, the velocity change is added: $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{a}t$.
The factor $\frac{1}{2}$ belongs to the displacement term for constant acceleration, not the velocity equation. Integrating constant acceleration once gives $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{a}t$.
Acceleration contributes a velocity change proportional to $t$, not $t^2$. The squared-time term appears when velocity is integrated to obtain position, so $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{a}t$.

cards.front: With constant acceleration, what is the position vector at time \(t\)?

options.explanation: Integrating $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{a}t$ gives displacement $\mathbf{u}t+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$. Adding the initial position $\mathbf{r}_0$ gives the position vector at time $t$.
The factor $\frac{1}{2}$ is lost if the acceleration term is not integrated correctly. Since $\int \mathbf{a}t\,dt=\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$, the correct coefficient is one half.
The sign of the acceleration vector should not be changed arbitrarily. Integrating the given acceleration produces $+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$; any direction is already encoded in $\mathbf{a}$.

Initial velocity contributes displacement proportional to $t$, whereas constant acceleration contributes displacement proportional to $t^2$. The correct position is $\mathbf{r}_0+\mathbf{u}t+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$.

cards.front: A direction vector gives the [ ___ ], not necessarily the velocity itself.
cards.back: A direction vector gives the ratio of components, not necessarily the velocity itself.

options.explanation: Parallel vectors are scalar multiples, so their corresponding components remain in a fixed proportion. A direction vector specifies this proportion without fixing the vector’s magnitude.
A direction vector does not determine how large the velocity is; the speed is needed for that. It specifies the ratio between corresponding components of the velocity.
A direction vector need not have magnitude one, so it is not automatically a unit vector. Its essential information is the ratio of its components.
Acceleration describes the rate of change of velocity and cannot be inferred from a direction vector alone. The direction vector instead determines the ratio of velocity components.

cards.front: How do you convert speed \(s\) in direction vector \(\mathbf{d}\) into velocity?

options.explanation: Dividing $\mathbf{d}$ by its magnitude produces a unit vector in the required direction. Multiplying that unit vector by $s$ gives a velocity whose magnitude is exactly $s$.
Multiplying directly by $\mathbf{d}$ gives magnitude $s|\mathbf{d}|$, not $s$, unless $\mathbf{d}$ is already a unit vector. The direction vector must first be divided by $|\mathbf{d}|$.
Multiplying by $|\mathbf{d}|$ increases the magnitude rather than normalising the direction. The required unit direction is $\mathbf{d}/|\mathbf{d}|$, which is then multiplied by $s$.
Dividing by the speed does not produce a velocity of magnitude $s$; it gives magnitude $|\mathbf{d}|/s$. Normalise $\mathbf{d}$ and then multiply by $s$.

cards.front: Given \(\mathbf{u}=12\mathbf{i}+16\mathbf{j}\) and \(\mathbf{v}=-5\mathbf{i}+18\mathbf{j}\) after 5 s, what is \(\mathbf{a}\)?

options.explanation: Constant acceleration is the velocity change divided by time. Here $\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}=-17\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}$, and dividing both components by $5$ gives the stated acceleration.
This reverses the velocity subtraction by calculating $\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}$. Acceleration uses $(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u})/5$, giving $-\frac{17}{5}\mathbf{i}+\frac{2}{5}\mathbf{j}\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
This gives the change in velocity but omits division by the elapsed $5$ seconds. Dividing $-17\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}$ by $5$ gives the correct acceleration.

Adding the initial and final velocities is not how acceleration is found. Subtract the initial velocity from the final velocity, then divide by $5$, obtaining $-\frac{17}{5}\mathbf{i}+\frac{2}{5}\mathbf{j}\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

cards.front: A vector perpendicular to \(\mathbf{i}\) has \(\mathbf{i}\)-component [ ___ ].
cards.back: A vector perpendicular to \(\mathbf{i}\) has \(\mathbf{i}\)-component zero.

options.explanation: Perpendicular vectors have zero scalar product. Since $\mathbf{i}\boldsymbol{\cdot}(a\mathbf{i}+b\mathbf{j})=a$, perpendicularity to $\mathbf{i}$ requires the coefficient $a$ to vanish.
A component of one would give a non-zero scalar product with $\mathbf{i}$, so the vectors would not be perpendicular. The $\mathbf{i}$-component must be zero.
Any non-zero $\mathbf{i}$-component creates a component parallel to $\mathbf{i}$ and a non-zero scalar product. Perpendicularity therefore requires an $\mathbf{i}$-component of zero.
The component is fully determined by the perpendicularity condition rather than being undefined. A zero scalar product with $\mathbf{i}$ forces the $\mathbf{i}$-component to be zero.

cards.front: For motion in the direction \(\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}\), what relation must the velocity components satisfy?

options.explanation: Any velocity in direction $\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}$ is a scalar multiple $\lambda\mathbf{i}+2\lambda\mathbf{j}$. Its $\mathbf{j}$-component must therefore be twice its $\mathbf{i}$-component.
This reverses the component ratio. The direction $\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}$ has component ratio $1:2$, so the $\mathbf{j}$-component is twice the $\mathbf{i}$-component.
Equal components describe a direction parallel to $\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}$, not $\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}$. The required component ratio is $1:2$.
The components must be proportional, not differ by a fixed additive amount. For direction $\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}$, the second component equals twice the first.

cards.front: For \(\mathbf{v}=(4t-8)\mathbf{i}+(3t+1)\mathbf{j}\), when is motion in direction \(\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}\)?

options.explanation: The required direction has $\mathbf{j}$-component twice the $\mathbf{i}$-component. Solving $3t+1=2(4t-8)$ gives $3t+1=8t-16$, hence $t=17/5$.
This results from reversing the required component relationship. The correct equation is $3t+1=2(4t-8)$, because the $\mathbf{j}$-component must be twice the $\mathbf{i}$-component, giving $t=17/5$.
This comes from mishandling the constant when expanding $2(4t-8)$. The expansion is $8t-16$, so solving $3t+1=8t-16$ gives $t=17/5$.
This treats the two velocity components as equal, which would give direction $\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}$. The required ratio is $1:2$, so $3t+1=2(4t-8)$ and $t=17/5$.

cards.front: To find a minimum speed, minimise [ ___ ] to avoid square roots.
cards.back: To find a minimum speed, minimise the square of the speed to avoid square roots.

options.explanation: Minimising the square of the speed gives the same minimum time as minimising speed because speed is non-negative, while avoiding differentiation of a square-root expression.
Minimising velocity treats a vector as though it were a scalar and does not define minimum speed. The square of the speed should be minimised because it is scalar and avoids square roots.
Minimising acceleration does not generally locate the minimum speed, especially when acceleration is constant. Instead, minimise the square of the speed, which has the same minimum as speed itself.

Minimising the reciprocal reverses the optimisation: a smaller reciprocal corresponds to a larger non-zero speed. Minimise the square of the speed to preserve the required minimum without square roots.

cards.front: For \(V^2=25t^2-58t+65\), when is speed minimum?

options.explanation: The quadratic reaches its minimum at its vertex, where $t=-b/(2a)=58/(2\times25)=29/25$. Since the coefficient of $t^2$ is positive, this is a minimum.
This results from dividing $58$ by $2$ twice when applying the vertex formula. Using $t=-b/(2a)$ gives $t=58/50=29/25$.
This omits the factor of $2$ in the denominator of the quadratic vertex formula. The correct calculation is $t=58/(2\times25)=29/25$.
The sign has been mishandled in $t=-b/(2a)$. Here $b=-58$, so $-b$ is positive and the minimum occurs at $t=29/25$.

cards.front: With constant acceleration, minimum speed occurs when velocity is [ ___ ] to acceleration, if the time is allowed.
cards.back: With constant acceleration, minimum speed occurs when velocity is perpendicular to acceleration, if the time is allowed.

options.explanation: Since $\frac{d}{dt}(|\mathbf{v}|^2)=2\mathbf{v}\mathbin{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}\mathbf{a}$, stationary speed occurs when the dot product is zero, meaning velocity and acceleration are perpendicular.

Parallel velocity and acceleration have a non-zero dot product, so the speed is changing rather than stationary. Minimum speed occurs when velocity is perpendicular to acceleration, provided that time is permitted.
Opposite velocity and acceleration mean the particle is slowing down, but speed has not yet necessarily reached its minimum. The minimum occurs when velocity becomes perpendicular to acceleration.

Equal velocity and acceleration is dimensionally inappropriate because they have different units, and it does not identify a speed minimum. The required geometric condition is that they are perpendicular.

cards.front: How do you find the position of \(B\) relative to \(A\)?

options.explanation: Subtracting the position vector of \(A\) from that of \(B\) gives the displacement from \(A\) to \(B\), which is the position of \(B\) relative to \(A\).
Reversing the subtraction gives the position of \(A\) relative to \(B\), pointing in the opposite direction. For \(B\) relative to \(A\), use \(\mathbf{r}_{B/A}=\mathbf{r}_B-\mathbf{r}_A\).
Adding the position vectors does not produce a displacement between the particles. Relative position is found by subtracting the reference position: \(\mathbf{r}_{B/A}=\mathbf{r}_B-\mathbf{r}_A\).
Subtracting \(B\)'s position from itself always gives the zero vector, regardless of \(A\). The required displacement from \(A\) to \(B\) is \(\mathbf{r}_B-\mathbf{r}_A\).

cards.front: What condition must hold for two objects to collide in 2D?
cards.back: Both components of \(\mathbf{r}_{B/A}\) are zero at the same time.

options.text: Both components of \(\mathbf{r}_{B/A}\) are zero at the same time.
options.explanation: A collision requires the objects to occupy the same horizontal and vertical coordinates simultaneously. Therefore, both components of their relative position vector must equal zero at one common time.

options.text: Either component of \(\mathbf{r}_{B/A}\) is zero at any time.
options.explanation: One zero component only shows that the objects share one coordinate, so they may still be separated in the other direction. Both relative-position components must be zero simultaneously.

options.text: Both components of \(\mathbf{r}_{B/A}\) are zero at different times.
options.explanation: The components becoming zero at different times means the objects separately share each coordinate, but never necessarily share one position. Both components must be zero at the same time.

options.text: Both components of \(\mathbf{r}_{B/A}\) are equal at the same time.
options.explanation: Equal relative-position components can both be non-zero, leaving a definite separation between the objects. For a collision, both components of the relative position must equal zero simultaneously.

cards.front: In variable vector kinematics, [ ___ ]{dt}\)}} and [ ___ ]{dt}\)}}.

options.explanation: Velocity is the time derivative of position, and acceleration is the time derivative of velocity. These vector derivative relationships apply component by component in variable kinematics.

This reverses both derivative relationships. Differentiating position gives velocity and differentiating velocity gives acceleration, rather than obtaining position and velocity by differentiating later quantities.
The first relationship is correct, but differentiating acceleration gives jerk rather than velocity. Acceleration is found by differentiating velocity: $\mathbf{a}=d\mathbf{v}/dt$.
Acceleration is not the time derivative of position; that derivative is velocity. The correct chain is $\mathbf{v}=d\mathbf{r}/dt$ followed by $\mathbf{a}=d\mathbf{v}/dt$.

cards.front: When integrating in vector kinematics, how are the constants found?

options.explanation: Integration introduces a constant vector, or a constant for each component. Substituting the stated initial or boundary conditions determines these constants uniquely.
Setting every constant to zero silently assumes zero initial values, which may not be given. The constants must instead be determined by substituting the given conditions.
Differentiating can check an antiderivative but eliminates constants, so it cannot determine their values. The values come from applying the given initial or boundary conditions.

Comparing vector components is part of the calculation but does not supply missing initial information. Integration constants are found by substituting the given conditions into the integrated expression.

cards.front: If given \(\mathbf{v}(t)\) and asked for distance between two positions, what is the method?
cards.back: Integrate velocity to get displacement.Take the magnitude of displacement.

options.text: Integrate velocity to get displacement.Take the magnitude of displacement.
options.explanation: Integrating the velocity vector over the interval gives the displacement vector between the positions. Its magnitude is the straight-line distance separating those two positions.

options.text: Differentiate velocity to get acceleration.Take the magnitude of acceleration.
options.explanation: Differentiating velocity gives acceleration, whose magnitude does not measure the separation of two positions. Instead, integrate velocity to obtain displacement and then take its magnitude.

options.text: Integrate velocity to get displacement.Take the sum of its components.
options.explanation: Adding displacement components does not give a vector’s magnitude and can cause cancellation. After integrating velocity, use the resultant magnitude, such as $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ in two dimensions.

options.text: Take the magnitude of velocity.Integrate it over the interval.
options.explanation: Integrating speed gives total path length, which may exceed the straight-line distance between the two positions. Integrate velocity first, then take the magnitude of the resulting displacement.
